## R Markdown

#1. Introduction

This project examines daily motor vehicle collisions in New York City using time-series analysis and forecasting techniques. The objective is to identify long-term trends, weekly and annual seasonal patterns, and changes in collision frequency.

The analysis evaluates Seasonal Naïve, Exponential Smoothing (ETS), Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), ARIMA with explanatory variables (ARIMAX), and Time Series Linear Models (TSLM).

Forecast performance is evaluated using a chronological training and testing design. Observations from 2012 through 2024 are used for model estimation, while 2025 is reserved for out-of-sample evaluation.

#2. Data Preparation and Data Quality
#2.1 Load Required Libraries
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(lubridate)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
```
#2.2 Import the Dataset

```{r}
library(janitor)

crashes <- readr::read_csv(
  
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names()

glimpse(crashes)
names(crashes)
```
#2.3 Convert Dates and Prepare Daily Observations

Each row represents an individual collision. The records are aggregated into daily collision counts.

```{r}
# STEP 1: Convert crash dates
crashes <- crashes |>
  mutate(
    day = lubridate::mdy(crash_date)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(day))

# STEP 2: Aggregate daily collision counts
crash_ts <- crashes |>
  count(day, name = "crashes") |>
  as_tsibble(index = day) |>
  fill_gaps(.full = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    crashes = replace_na(crashes, 0)
  )

# STEP 3: Inspect dataset
glimpse(crash_ts)

# STEP 4: Check date range
range(crash_ts$day)

# STEP 5: Count observations
nrow(crash_ts)

# STEP 6: Check missing values
sum(is.na(crash_ts$crashes))

# STEP 7: Check duplicate dates
anyDuplicated(crash_ts$day)
```

The daily time series is constructed by counting collision records for each date. Missing calendar dates are included in the time index and assigned zero recorded collisions

#2.4 Exploratory Time-Series Plot

```{r}
crash_ts |>
  autoplot(crashes) +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Daily Motor Vehicle Collisions",
    subtitle = "July 2012 through the latest available observation",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  )
```

#2.5 Descriptive Statistics
```{r}
crash_ts |>
  as_tibble() |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    average_crashes = mean(crashes),
    median_crashes = median(crashes),
    standard_deviation = sd(crashes),
    minimum_crashes = min(crashes),
    maximum_crashes = max(crashes)
  )
```

#3. Training and Testing Data
The training dataset covers January 2012 through December 2024. The testing dataset covers January through December 2025.

The chronological split prevents future observations from being used during model estimation.

```{r}
train <- crash_ts |>
  filter_index("2012-01-01" ~ "2024-12-31") |>
  mutate(
    trend = row_number(),
    weekday = factor(
      wday(day),
      levels = 1:7,
      labels = c(
        "Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday",
        "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday",
        "Saturday"
      )
    )
  )

test <- crash_ts |>
  filter_index("2025-01-01" ~ "2025-12-31") |>
  mutate(
    trend = row_number() + nrow(train),
    weekday = factor(
      wday(day),
      levels = 1:7,
      labels = c(
        "Sunday", "Monday", "Tuesday",
        "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday",
        "Saturday"
      )
    )
  )

# Verify observations
nrow(train)
nrow(test)

range(train$day)
range(test$day)

# Check weekday distribution
table(train$weekday)
table(test$weekday)

# Confirm complete testing period
stopifnot(nrow(test) == 365)
```

The trend variable provides a continuous sequential index across the training and testing periods. The weekday variable identifies recurring weekly patterns.

```{r}
weekday_chart
```

#4.2 Weekdays Versus Weekends
```{r}
weekday_weekend <- train |>
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      lubridate::wday(day, week_start = 1) <= 5,
      "Weekday",

    day_type = factor(

      levels = c("Weekday", "Weekend")

  group_by(day_type) |>
  summarise(
    average_crashes = mean(crashes, na.rm = TRUE),
    total_crashes = sum(crashes, na.rm = TRUE),

    .groups = "drop"

weekday_weekend
```

#interpretation
Weekdays Versus Weekends

The weekday-versus-weekend analysis examines differences in average daily motor vehicle collisions in New York City. Daily collision counts were grouped into weekdays (Monday through Friday) and weekends (Saturday and Sunday), and the average number of collisions was calculated for each group.

The comparison provides insight into how traffic activity and collision frequency vary across the weekly cycle. Differences between the two groups may reflect variations in commuting patterns, travel behavior, and recreational activity.

These findings support the inclusion of weekday effects in the time-series forecasting models, allowing the analysis to account for systematic differences in collision frequency across the days of the week.

#5. Stationarity and Time-Series Diagnostics
Stationarity is important when developing ARIMA forecasting models. The analysis uses visual inspection, autocorrelation plots, and formal stationarity tests to investigate the characteristics of daily collision counts.
#5.1 Time-Series Display

```{r}
train |>
  gg_tsdisplay(
    crashes,
    plot_type = "partial",
    lag_max = 35
  )
```

#5.2 KPSS Stationarity Test
```{r}
train |>
  features(
    crashes,
    unitroot_kpss
  )
```

The KPSS test evaluates the null hypothesis that the series is stationary. A small p-value provides evidence against stationarity.

#5.3 Determine Differencing Requirements
```{r}
# Regular differencing
train |>
  features(
    crashes,
    unitroot_ndiffs
  )

# Seasonal differencing
train |>
  features(
    crashes,
    unitroot_nsdiffs
  )
```
The differencing recommendations help identify whether regular or seasonal differencing may be appropriate for ARIMA modeling.

#6. ETS Forecasting Models
Exponential Smoothing models estimate the level, trend, and seasonal components of a time series.

This analysis evaluates an additive ETS specification and an automatically selected ETS model.

```{r}
  ets_models <- train |>
  model(
    ETS_Additive = ETS(
      crashes ~ error("A") +
        trend("A") +
        season("A")
    ),

    ETS_Automatic = ETS(crashes)
  )

# Model summaries
report(ets_models)
```
An additive ETS specification is used as a benchmark. The automatic ETS model selects an appropriate exponential smoothing structure based on the training data.

A multiplicative seasonal model can also be considered if the observations are strictly positive and the model is appropriate for the data.

#6.1 ETS Forecasts
```{r}
ets_fc <- ets_models |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

autoplot(
  ets_fc,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "ETS Model Forecast Comparison",
    subtitle = "NYC Daily Motor Vehicle Collisions: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions",
    color = "ETS Model"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

#6.2 ETS Accuracy
```{r}
ets_accuracy <- accuracy(
  ets_fc,
  test
) |>
  select(
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE,
    MASE
  ) |>
  arrange(RMSE)

ets_accuracy
```

#7. ARIMA Forecasting
ARIMA models capture temporal dependence through autoregressive, differencing, and moving-average components.

#7.1 Automatic ARIMA Model

```{r}
arima_auto <- train |>
  model(
    ARIMA_Automatic = ARIMA(crashes)
  )

report(arima_auto)

tidy(arima_auto)
```

Automatic ARIMA selection identifies a suitable model based on the training data.

#7.2 ARIMA Residual Diagnostics

```{r}
arima_auto |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
arima_auto |>
  augment() |>
  features(
    .innov,
    ljung_box,
    lag = 14,
    dof = 0
  )
```

The Ljung-Box test evaluates whether residual autocorrelation remains. A small p-value suggests that the residuals contain additional temporal structure.

The degrees of freedom should be adjusted to reflect the estimated ARMA parameters when conducting the formal model-specific test. The value above is a conservative initial diagnostic, not a universal degrees-of-freedom choice.

#7.3 ARIMA Forecasts
```{r}
arima_fc <- arima_auto |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

autoplot(
  arima_fc,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "Automatic ARIMA Forecasts",
    subtitle = "NYC Daily Motor Vehicle Collisions: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  )
```

#7.4 ARIMA Accuracy

```{r}
arima_accuracy <- accuracy(
  arima_fc,
  test
) |>
  select(
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE,
    MASE
  )

arima_accuracy
```

#8. ARIMAX Forecasting Model
ARIMAX extends ARIMA by including explanatory variables. This analysis incorporates a linear trend, weekday indicators, and Fourier terms to represent annual seasonality.

Fourier terms are constructed using sine and cosine functions with an annual period of approximately 365.25 days.

#8.1 Create Fourier Variables

```{r}
train_x <- train |>
  mutate(
    fourier_1 = sin(2 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_2 = cos(2 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_3 = sin(4 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_4 = cos(4 * pi * trend / 365.25)
  )

test_x <- test |>
  mutate(
    fourier_1 = sin(2 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_2 = cos(2 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_3 = sin(4 * pi * trend / 365.25),
    fourier_4 = cos(4 * pi * trend / 365.25)
  )
```

#8.2 Fit ARIMAX
```{r}
arimax_model <- train_x |>
  model(
    ARIMAX = ARIMA(
      crashes ~ trend +
        weekday +
        fourier_1 +
        fourier_2 +
        fourier_3 +
        fourier_4
    )
  )

report(arimax_model)

tidy(arimax_model)
```
#8.3 ARIMAX Residual Diagnostics

```{r}
arimax_model |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

```{r}
arimax_model |>
  augment() |>
  features(
    .innov,
    ljung_box,
    lag = 14,
    dof = 0
  )
```

As with the automatic ARIMA model, the degrees of freedom should be refined using the fitted ARIMA error structure.

#8.4 ARIMAX Forecasts

```{r}
arimax_fc <- arimax_model |>
  forecast(new_data = test_x)

autoplot(
  arimax_fc,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "ARIMAX Forecasts of NYC Daily Collisions",
    subtitle = "2025 Testing Period",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  ) 
```

#8.5 ARIMAX Accuracy
```{r}
arimax_accuracy <- accuracy(
  arimax_fc,
  test
) |>
  select(
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE,
    MASE
  )

arimax_accuracy
```

#9. TSLM Forecasting Models
Time Series Linear Models provide an interpretable approach to modeling temporal trends and seasonal patterns.

Three specifications are evaluated.

#9.1 Trend-Only Model
The first model incorporates a linear time trend to examine the overall direction of daily collision frequency.

```{r}
fit_trend <- train |>
  model(
    Trend_Only = TSLM(
      crashes ~ trend
    )
  )

report(fit_trend)
```
#Residual Diagnostics
```{r}
fit_trend |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

#Forecasts

```{r}
forecast_trend <- fit_trend |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

autoplot(
  forecast_trend,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Daily Motor Vehicle Collision Forecast",
    subtitle = "Trend-Only TSLM Model: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  ) 
```

#Accuracy
```{r}
accuracy_trend <- accuracy(
  forecast_trend,
  test
)

accuracy_trend
```
#9.2 Trend and Weekly Seasonality Model
The second specification incorporates weekday indicators to capture differences in collision frequency across the seven days of the week.

```{r}
fit_trend_seasonal <- train |>
  model(
    Trend_Weekly = TSLM(
      crashes ~ trend + weekday
    )
  )

report(fit_trend_seasonal)
```

#Residual Diagnostics
```{r}
fit_trend_seasonal |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

#Forecasts
```{r}
forecast_seasonal <- fit_trend_seasonal |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

autoplot(
  forecast_seasonal,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Daily Motor Vehicle Collision Forecast",
    subtitle = "Trend and Weekly Seasonality Model: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  ) 
```
#Accuracy

```{r}
accuracy_seasonal <- accuracy(
  forecast_seasonal,
  test
)

accuracy_seasonal
```

#9.3 Full TSLM: Trend, Weekly and Annual Seasonality
The third model incorporates both weekday indicators and annual Fourier terms.

```{r}
fit_tslm_full <- train |>
  model(
    TSLM_Full = TSLM(
      crashes ~ trend +
        weekday +
        fourier(
          K = 5,
          period = 365.25
        )
    )
  )

report(fit_tslm_full)
```

#Residual Diagnostics
```{r}
fit_tslm_full |>
  gg_tsresiduals()
```

#Forecasts

```{r}
forecast_tslm_full <- fit_tslm_full |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

autoplot(
  forecast_tslm_full,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "Full TSLM Forecast of NYC Daily Collisions",
    subtitle = "Trend, Weekly and Annual Seasonality: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions"
  ) 
```

#Accuracy
```{r}
accuracy_tslm_full <- accuracy(
  forecast_tslm_full,
  test
)

accuracy_tslm_full
```

#10. Model Comparison
All forecasting models are evaluated using the same testing period. This provides a consistent basis for comparing their predictive performance.

#10.1 Fit the Benchmark Models
The seasonal naïve model provides a useful benchmark by repeating the previous week's observations.

```{r}
fits <- train |>
  model(
    Seasonal_Naive = SNAIVE(
      crashes ~ lag("week")
    ),

    ETS_Additive = ETS(
      crashes ~ error("A") +
        trend("A") +
        season("A")
    ),

    ETS_Automatic = ETS(crashes),

    ARIMA_Automatic = ARIMA(crashes),

    ARIMAX = ARIMA(
      crashes ~ trend +
        weekday +
        fourier(
          K = 5,
          period = 365.25
        )
    ),

    TSLM_Full = TSLM(
      crashes ~ trend +
        weekday +
        fourier(
          K = 5,
          period = 365.25
        )
    )
  )

report(fits)
```

#10.2 Generate Forecasts
```{r}
fc <- fits |>
  forecast(new_data = test)

fc
```
#10.3 Calculate Forecast Accuracy

```{r}
final_accuracy <- accuracy(
  fc,
  test
) |>
  select(
    .model,
    RMSE,
    MAE,
    MAPE,
    MASE,
    ACF1
  ) |>
  arrange(RMSE)

final_accuracy
```

Lower RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MASE values indicate better forecasting performance. ACF1 provides information about first-order residual autocorrelation.

#10.4 Identify the Best Forecasting Model
```{r}
best_model <- final_accuracy |>
  slice_min(
    RMSE,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

best_model
```

Model selection should consider forecast accuracy alongside residual diagnostics and model interpretability.

#10.5 Plot Forecast Comparisons
```{r}
autoplot(
  fc,
  crash_ts |> filter_index("2025")
) +
  labs(
    title = "Comparison of NYC Daily Collision Forecasts",
    subtitle = "Six Forecasting Specifications: 2025",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Daily Collisions",
    color = "Forecast Model"
  ) 
```

#11. TSLM Model Explanatory Power
R-squared measures the proportion of variation explained by a fitted regression model. It is an in-sample measure and should not be confused with out-of-sample forecast accuracy.
```{r}
glance(fit_trend)
glance(fit_trend_seasonal)
glance(fit_tslm_full)
```

Use the actual R-squared values returned above when preparing the final presentation.

#12. Road-User Injury Analysis
In addition to collision frequency, the original dataset contains injury information for pedestrians, cyclists, and motor vehicle occupants.

The following section aggregates daily injury counts separately for each road-user group.

```{r}
road_user_daily <- crashes |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(
    ped_injured = sum(
      number_of_pedestrians_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    cyc_injured = sum(
      number_of_cyclist_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mot_injured = sum(
      number_of_motorist_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

If your CSV uses different injury column names, replace them with the exact names returned by names(crashes).

#12.1 Road-User Injury Time Series

```{r}
# Aggregate daily injuries by road-user category

road_user_daily <- crashes |>
  group_by(day) |>
  summarise(
    ped_injured = sum(
      number_of_pedestrians_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    cyc_injured = sum(
      number_of_cyclist_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    mot_injured = sum(
      number_of_motorist_injured,
      na.rm = TRUE
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```
This analysis provides additional context about the distribution of traffic-related injuries across road-user groups. Collision counts and injury counts represent different outcomes and should be interpreted separately.

```{r}
road_user_chart <- road_user_daily |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      ped_injured,
      cyc_injured,
      mot_injured
    ),
    names_to = "road_user",
    values_to = "injuries"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    road_user = recode(
      road_user,
      ped_injured = "Pedestrians",
      cyc_injured = "Cyclists",
      mot_injured = "Motor Vehicle Occupants"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = day,
      y = injuries,
      color = road_user
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~road_user,
    scales = "free_y",
    ncol = 1
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Pedestrians" = "steelblue",
      "Cyclists" = "darkorange",
      "Motor Vehicle Occupants" = "forestgreen"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "NYC Traffic Injuries by Road User",
    subtitle = "Daily injuries among pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Number of Injuries",
    color = "Road User"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 14
    ),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10),
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

road_user_chart
```

#Calculate total injuries by road-user category
This additional analysis will be useful for your project report.

```{r}
road_user_summary <- road_user_daily |>
```

#14. Conclusion
This analysis examines daily motor vehicle collisions in New York City using historical observations beginning in 2012. The forecasting framework evaluates several statistical approaches, including Seasonal Naïve, ETS, ARIMA, ARIMAX, and TSLM.

The TSLM specifications progressively incorporate a linear trend, weekday indicators, and annual Fourier terms. This allows the analysis to examine the contribution of long-term changes and recurring seasonal patterns to daily collision frequency.

Forecast performance is assessed using the 2025 testing period, with RMSE, MAE, MAPE, and MASE providing measures of predictive accuracy. Residual diagnostics are also used to examine whether temporal dependence remains unexplained.

The final model selection should be based on the actual out-of-sample accuracy results and residual behavior rather than in-sample R-squared alone.

The road-user injury analysis provides an additional perspective by examining differences in injury patterns among pedestrians, cyclists, and motor vehicle occupants.

Overall, the project provides a structured framework for understanding historical collision patterns and evaluating statistical forecasting approaches. The findings may help inform further research into urban traffic safety, temporal collision patterns, and the distribution of traffic-related injuries.

6. Important things to check before knitting
There are four things I particularly want you to verify.

1. Dataset column names: Run names(crashes) to confirm the three injury columns in Section 12. NYC's dataset uses specific field names, and these must match exactly.

2. ETS seasonality: Check the model reports to confirm the seasonal structure selected for daily observations. Your data have a weekly cycle, so a seven-day seasonal pattern is particularly important.

3. MAPE: Daily collision counts should be positive for ordinary MAPE interpretation. If any actual testing observations are zero, MAPE can be undefined or misleading. MAE and RMSE remain useful.

4. ARIMA computation: Automatic ARIMA estimation on more than 4,500 daily observations can take time. Start with the default automatic selection before trying exhaustive model searches.
